item.title: What do LLMs Really Learn About Model Weights? A Stratification Approach to Examine Weight Space Programming
item.description:
TLDR

I attempted to replicate “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming” by Takehi et al (2026) with stratification on two reasoning models, GPT 6 Astra and Deepseek-V4.1-Flash. The task for the LLMs is to identify the game a ML model is trained for giving the weight of the model (using exact same prompt and weight defined by Takehi).

Although both of these models do well on the surface (4/4 correct for Astra and 3/4 correct for Flash), the stratification approach exposes the difference in mechanism between these two models in approaching the problem. The experiment result shows that Flash depends a lot on channel label for the answer (while Astra's performance does not degrade when channel label does not present). Additionally, Astra is able to identify the game with good accuracy using only the first layer of weight or as few as 1000 weight values selected at random out of 17253 weight values (Flash's performance degrade substantially on these).

So Astra survives this first round of stratification tests just for now. Comparing the results between Astra and Flash, it is obvious that Flash is relying heavily on prompt metadata instead of reading the weights.

Background

On November 2 an article “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming” was published by Takehi et al (2026). The article is cleanly written and one of the claims is that by looking at model weights, GPT 6 Astra can tell what the model is trained to do. The article reports that Astra is able to name the game a ML model is trained for in four different cases (Breakout, Pong, Pac-man, Freeway) directly through the weight of the model without use of external tools.

If LLMs do have capability to read model weights and identify what it is trained to do, this would have huge implications in the fields of interpretability and weight auditing without evaluation as suggested by the article by Takehi et al (2026).

I find the reported results to be very surprising, so I attempted to replicate their experiment using exactly the same prompt and model weights on two models, GPT 6 Astra, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Surprisingly they all did decently well on the surface.


So the next question is why LLM is able to figure that out. I did a full set of stratification control experiments for DeepSeek V4.1-Flash and GPT-6-Astra to gain more insights.

Methodology

Setup of experiment

For the replication, I construct the same prompt and use the same model weight found in Takehi’s released log repo as the ground truth. 

Models in scope

Gpt-6-astra. Reasoning effort = medium. Temperature T=1 (unfortunately cannot change this value)

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Temperature T=0.7

Stratification variants (each variant changes one aspect of the prompt):

  1. Real (exactly same as Takehi's log repo)
  2. Shuffled: the position of the weights is randomly permuted, the values are preserved
  3. No weight: Only prompt meta data remains
  4. Anonymous channels: 
    1. Example prompt before: The 10*10 grid in 5 channels: agent, moving objects, reward targets, obstacles, previous frame
    2. Example prompt after: : The 10*10 grid in 5 channels: channel 0, channel 1, channel 2, channel 3, channel 4
  5. Untrained: Weight is randomly initialized
  6. Layer sweep (w1_only, w3_only): only one of the three weight matrices is given, the others are not.
  7. Random 1000: We keep 1000 random weight values of 17253 total weight values, the other 16253 weight values are zeroed
  8. Top 50 per channel: We keep 50 largest magnitude weights per channel, 250 in total, the rest of 17003 weight values zeroed.

Sampling Strategy

For each of the variant we estimate the probability of the model answering the correct game label with the model information. For each experiment we sample n=15. Because this sample size is small, it is a limitation of this experiment, we apply Wilson 95% confidence interval.

Results

Under every stratification experiments I conducted, Astra shows strong performance even without channel labels or with just partial weights (random 1000 weight values, top 50 weight values, or just one layer of weights). When the weight values are randomly initialized, Astra refuses to answer or name a game, while Flash tries to name a game in the answer 14/60 of the times (out of these 14 cases, 9 are Pac-Man, and 5 are Freeway).

Another interesting observation is that Astra is able to recognize the game correctly even with just the first layer W1 of the weights of the game, while Flash takes a severe degradation in performance when only W1 is present. It seems that Flash finds slightly more signals in W3 (40%) than W1 (30%) (not statistically significant), and Astra capture signals more reliably in input feature weights W1 (100%) than output logit weight W3 (62%).

The second question is whether the signals in the weights is in the numerical values or the structure. To find this out I conduct the experiment that shuffles the weight values before passing them to the model to see if the game can still be identified. In this case Astra refuses to answer a game 52/60 times, names a game 8/60 times, and gets correct in Freeway 1 time. Flash on the other hand, refuses to answer 39/60 times, answer 21/60 times, and get 5 correct in Pac-Man.

I believe that the 5 correct cases that Flash get correct is a prior for Flash here, as in 78.6% of the cases, Flash answers Pac-Man when there is no signal presented (in shuffled/no weight/untrained variants of the experiment).

Discussion

The stratification experiments show that although Flash scores 3/4 on the surface in naming the game for the model correctly, its mechanism heavily relies on channel labels and prior for Pac-Man. Its performance takes a severe hit when channel labels are replaced. And it trends to guess Pac-Man when there is not sufficient signals present.

Astra on the other hand takes little performance hit (if not none) when channel labels are missing, or when only partial weight values are presented. Additionally Astra, compared to Flash, is more likely to refuse to name a game in its answer when no signal is presented. Overall Astra is performing well under this stratification experiment for this specific task of naming games for the four models.

It should also be noted that Astra picks up signals more reliably in W1 than W3. One or both of the following interpretations can be true:

  1. Astra has better capability in recognizing input feature weights than output feature weights. This is a possible interpretation.
  2. In the setup of some of the models for the tasks, W1 contains more quality signals than W3. This is quite possible because there is a big asymmetric in weight value count, W1 has 16000 weight values, while W3 has just 160.

It would be really interesting to validate if interpretation 1 is true for future experiments.

Limitations and Next Steps

  • Small sample size for N=15 (API is costly, but will try to bump this)
  • All 4 tasks and Weights are reused from original experiment by Takehi et al, will be nice to include more originally trained weights and tasks to further validate model capability.
  • Can include a wider range of models in the stratification experiments in the future (for example, Claude Fable, plus more open models as they are less of a black box)

Conclusion

In conclusion, the stratification methodology in this experiment helps separate the difference in capability for Astra and Flash in model identification tasks described in “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming” by Takehi et al (2026). I believe stratification can help to uncover the mechanism behind the surprises of weight-space programming and hope to see this as a standard part of future work in this space.

Related Work

Within three days of Takehi et al.'s release, independent replications and critiques have started appearing. Simon Willison ran Qwen 3.8 27B locally on Nov 3 and reported similar Pac-Man prior-lock pattern. In that experiment, Qwen named the Freeway network "a simplified Pac-Man-like grid game," suggesting the behavior might possibly generalizes beyond Deepseek in this experiment. The stratification angle in this post is, as far as I can tell, the first to apply control variants systematically to the raw-weight reading claim.

Reproducibility

Full code, data, and run JSONs are available at github.com/CCaptainX/wsp-replication.

Acknowledgements

Thanks to Takehi, Teoh, Zhang and Khattab for publishing "Sparks of Weight-Space Programming" together with a complete log repository. The byte-identical prompt reconstruction, and this entire replication, is only possible because of their reproducibility discipline.

item.title: Rhythm Stage Setup v5
item.description:
I recently finished the largest set of changes I've made to my rhythm stage setup in 4.5y. The basic interface is similar, but I have a lot more flexibility, more control, more options, and it's easier to travel with. My favorite part is the speech recognition for calling chords.

I started off playing mandolin and piano, and then over the years added progressively more expressive footdrums. I added a breath controller. I built out a complex but expressive system where these different interfaces could interact to let me produce a coherent rhythm section. After a frustrating experience moving from one Mac to another and wanting to simplify, I moved from the Mac to a Raspberry Pi, set it all up as a pedalboard, and then again as a lighter pedalboard.

During the last year and a bit, however, I haven't been tinkering. It did what I wanted, in a reliable and portable fashion. And it was hard to modify: the pedalboard was static, and the Raspberry Pi code wasn't easy to get at either. Which was fine, and probably good for me! I just played a lot of gigs (23 Kingfisher, 3 Free Raisins, 3 Dandelion) and got better at it.

But then it started breaking. My whistle synth box didn't always come up, the drums sometimes needed an external DI, and a USB sound card snapped. Flying back from Atlanta my gear suffered rough enough treatment to bend a USB B connector, and it was clear my system needed some love.

I started with the most urgent portion: the whistle synth. I had Claude port it over to my laptop, where I turned it into a Mac app. This also let me add several more voices, and a mute option that never made loud clicks (I'm not really a hardware person).

This project made me realize that AI getting capable meant that the tradeoffs around laptop-vs-embedded had shifted. I could have everything on my laptop, and without needing to put painfully large amounts of time into programming it could all be fully defined in code instead of manually-configured GUIs. Having it on my laptop would make it easy to apply models to modify and improve it, and open up a lot more lexibility.

I decided to move as much as possible over to the laptop. This meant no more Raspberry Pi, whistle synth box, physical switches for signal routing, and computer code instead of guitar pedals. I moved from:

To:

Four fewer pedals, three fewer DIs, two fewer power bricks, and no little computers. Saves ten pounds: 32lb to 22lb. The Mac weighs ~3.5lb, but I'm traveling with it regardless.

Of these savings, 3lb (2.7lb of talkbox + 0.3lb of power supply) was from giving up the talkbox. I liked how this simplified my setup, including less complex audio routing, but after playing Moondance both Cecilia and I really missed it. So I added it back:

A large benefit of moving to the Mac is I can now see what I'm doing. I control my rig with an external keyboard, covered in little labels that remind me what each key does:

For example, before playing Trip to Moscow I would probably press FB (footbass), S (make footbass play synth bass), FX (breath-controlled keyboard overlay), set the drums to custom kit 63 (electronic kit), and then press L (keyboard velocity-insensitive bass overlay) and change the keyboard to epiano2 when we got all electronic. And press JH (breath-controlled bass-following low bass) at some point partway through for more ability to pulse the offbeat. Without a monitor, I needed to keep this all clear in my head, which was especially important since many settings are modal or interact. I usually didn't mess up, but partly because I tried not to dial in anything with too many presses.

Now I can just represent the state on my monitor:

This is also very helpful for showing which voices apply to which instruments. Previously I needed to remember that on FX (breath-controlled overlay) the B key would give me a supersaw, while on Dc (chord drone) the B key was a different voice (I forget what). Now I can choose a set of voices for each instrument that are the ones that sound best with this kind of control, without worrying about how I'll remember which button gives me which sound.

This is basically all "what I had before, but easier to control". Which is good, but the real payoff comes from making it much easier to extend the system. I've done a lot here, with extensive help from Claude Code, and it's going to take me a bunch of time to learn how to play these new options well.

A big one is that because I now route my mandolin through the system I can replace pedals with code, add more effects than it was worth carrying pedals for, and write effects that consider what other things in the system are doing. This includes using the breath controller as an expression pedal, or tonal effects that care about the active chord. Demo video:

youtube

I also added speech recognition, where I can turn things on and off vocally, and even call chords. For chord calling I had Claude make me a custom speech recognizing system for the numbers one through seven (Nashville numbers) trained specifically on my voice and optimized for minimizing latency (decision in 40-170ms). It also runs Apple's in parallel, primarily to allow learning from mistakes but also to handle numbers the custom one misses and any non-number commands. Here's a video from earlier today, showing how I was still working to improve both my call timing and the code that triggers the changes; you can hear that many changes are off by a beat:

youtube

Here's a short updated video after a bunch of work this afternoon and evening to make number calling more reliable (af196263f). This involved adding a prior that chords run for a multiple of 2 beats on a grid implied by previous called chords, better word boundary identification, and a bunch of parameter tuning where I made recordings as I worked with it. I'm much happier with it now, and the two mis-timed changes in the video below are me calling early (0:59, 1:15):

youtube

I'm also trying to figure out new things I can do with the breath controller, and one thing I've been playing around with is percussion:

youtube

Other stuff:

  • Vocal effects, including ones like a vocoder that care about the currently active chord. Not sure I like any of these enough yet to use live.

  • Cecilia needs to hear my mandolin playing, but gets plenty of computer overlays in the monitor wash already. This was a problem with talkbox, which can be fed by either the mandolin or computer. Now that it's all running through my box, though, I can make talkbox go to the mandolin output channel if mandolin is included, and to the computer output channel otherwise.

  • I auditioned and added a lot more voices. Including adjusting which voices are available for which instrument by replacing some that didn't work with that instrument's method of articulation. I don't know if any of them are worth it yet, though: I still mostly do the small number of things I like.

  • I added French Canadian feet back into the system, after discarding them when I switched to the Raspberry Pi. They're no longer samples, but synthesized, which lets me use how hard I stomp or the breath controller to adjust how hard the hit is. I like these a lot, and used them live to good effect at the one gig I've done since this change.

  • I also added a "stompy feet" option which is feet with a bassier kick, a "bare feet" option with sounds synthesized to imitate my own bare feet, and a "hand drums" option which was a Claude "happy accident" that sounded interesting enough to keep. I'm not sure I'd actually use either of the second two, though.

  • When used stand-alone, the Focusrite 2i2 takes in a mic (whistle bass, calling chords) and mandolin and gives two channels (computer and mandolin + feet, though really it's "doesn't go to Cecilia's monitor" and "does go to Cecilia's monitor"). I've also added integration for my custom 1818VSL mixer, in which case you skip the 2i2, run the mic and mandolin into channels 1 and 2, and all my processing happens automatically before the mixer sees channels 1 and 2. Kind of an automatic effects loop.

  • I added recording to the custom VSL mixer, including logging MIDI signals and keyboard presses so it's easier to evaluate later (or tweak if we wanted to turn recordings into another live CD).

  • I'm toying with starting to run our own monitors by default with the VSL, since it has enough output channels to pass my normal outputs to the sound board and then also give a mix to each of us. I'd use XLR Y-cables on the other inputs so the board would also get a full copy of everything.

  • Outputs can now be stereo, in case we wanted to switch to in-ear monitors. But I really like stage wedges for feeling connected to the dancers: being responsive to them in the moment is, to me, a big part of the appeal of playing live for dancing. And it would be a fourth thing connected to my head (after the mic, talkbox tube, and breath controller) making me even more borg.

  • My keyboard (Yamaha P-121) includes USB audio support, and I already have it connected to my computer over USB for MIDI purposes. Using this stream avoids several lossy steps, and I've made the VSL mixer bring it on as an "input 9" when available. Sadly if I'm ever working with someone's P-125a keyboard, the "a" means that they dropped the USB audio feature.

  • I added a bunch of features with technocontra in mind (kick ducks, pads, weird effects) but I don't think I like any of them even for technocontra. Not sure yet.

  • I tried a version where whistling picks a chord, but didn't end up liking it at all.

  • One cool thing about a whistle-controlled synthesizer and speech recognition is that I can do both of them at once on the same mic: they're very easy to tell apart.

  • Overall, I'm still mostly playing live with only a small portion of the possibility space I've built for myself with this instrument. Some of this is that a lot of things that are possible turn out not to be very effective in a noisy dance hall, or just don't sound good anywhere. Some of this is that there are some very neat things that it's possible to do that I haven't practiced well enough to take advantage of. And some is that I just forget to try some things live.

  • When I switch to pedals choosing bass instead of being drums it now switches to a preset that's a better fit for that, so I press one button ("DCN": drum chooses note) instead of several ("DCN", "FB", "D", "v", "+", "+", "+", oct up).

This post took me way too long to get out, both because I keep adding to the system and because I'd rather make demo videos once I'm good at controlling the system. Since that kept resulting in not publishing, I've lowered my threshold to get something out. I can always follow up as I do more, and several of the ideas above would have been better as their own posts.

The code is all on github if you or your agent would like to look:

  • jammer: most of it
  • whistle-synth: the whistle-controlled synth
  • vsl1818: the custom mixing app

item.title: RSI explained
item.description:
Just how long will it be until AI can improve itself? (Also known as recursive self-improvement or RSI.)

Well, AI coding abilities have exploded in 2026. In May 2026, Anthropic merged 2,500 code changes per day within their organization. By September, they were merging over 30,000 per day. They had to replace Git in their internal mono repository to handle the load of all that AI generated code.


In fact, Claude is even leading model R&D. In February 2026, under 1% of their work was led by AI; by August, it was 26%. The definition of AI "leading" the work is that AI can complete most of the task end-to-end from a high-level prompt, while the human supervises (level AL4 from Epoch AI). Over 90% of their work is level AL3 or above ("AI collaborates"). This is quite a high level of autonomy, though Anthropic still claims that "Claude is not operating fully autonomously for any measured subset of AI R&D work" -- or claimed such, as of August.


On November 2nd, Anthropic amended their SEC S-1A filing one week after their initial public filing. One of the changes was the addition of the sentence, "our internal estimates [...] indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of 'dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.'" That's right, imminently. This is after researchers from both OpenAI and Anthropic have been saying that progress has been faster than they expected (Sept 2026).

On the same day, MIT researchers pointed GPT-6 Astra at the bare model weights of a small model, Qwen3.5-0.8B, and asked it to improve the model's performance. The Qwen model's MATH-500 accuracy went from 7.9% to 48.1%, and GSM8K accuracy went from 13.8% to 67.1%. This was mostly because Astra was able to cure the smaller model of getting stuck in loops (which, as I can attest, small Qwen models quite like doing). This is without a normal training pipeline, just the raw weights. I can imagine that with proper infrastructure, a model's ability to understand and improve itself could be extremely high.

Allow me to remind you that RSI, or more colourfully, an intelligence explosion, is utterly uncontrollable. We have been applying immense optimization pressure to these models through reinforcement learning and they learn to reward hack and carry out their goals at all costs (see Hugging Face). We have not solved AI alignment; they do not want the things we want them to want. We have no hope of solving AI control if we persist in leaving training clusters hooked up to the internet (!). These models can hack out of anything. They are expert-level already at biology (Anthropic has hooked up Claude to a wet lab to run experiments) and could easily engineer a super-pandemic, if they thought we were in their way.

RSI may not be a clear line in the sand; even Anthropic said that they may not be able to notice when their development significantly accelerates. From where I'm standing, the frog looks to be just about boiling.

item.title: The Logic of Disgust
item.description:
Content Warning: Contains graphic themes including bodily fluids, moral disgust, and sexual violence (discussed, not described). Maybe don't read over breakfast.


I found a book about disgust recently. W.I. Miller’s The Anatomy of Disgust [1]  is a serious academic work about vomit, faeces, and why other people’s smell is always worse than your own. Naturally, I was intrigued.

As someone into social psychology, I often encounter discussions about emotions influencing society: how anger can motivate political movements, or how social interactions are regulated by pride and shame. Disgust, meanwhile, is something I've mainly encountered as a biological matter rather than a social one. The book starts with its evolutionary function: recoil from dangerous pathogens and you are more likely to survive. So far, so logical. But then...  Then I met Catherine of Siena.

The Stories We Swallow

Catherine was a fourteenth-century caretaker tending a woman with a disgusting cancerous wound. The smell made Catherine retch. But rather than keeping her distance, she saw her nausea as a personal failure and was determined to correct it. Basically, she exposure-therapied herself by staying even closer. When the retching persisted, she escalated to an act that defied the logic of stay-alive biology: she collected the pus from the wound into a cup and drank it.

At this point I had to set the book aside and focus on my breathing to avoid becoming part of the subject matter in a public library.

How could one willingly swallow pus?

Well… there's a reasonable chance you've done so yourself today. 

Every morning, millions of people pour a white liquid into their coffee, their cereal and their children’s cups. It arrives cold, clean. The smell of the body it came from removed. Processing, distance and language change how we perceive what we consume significantly, allowing us to ignore the roughly one drop of pus per cup of bovine lactation. [2] Catherine drank from a wound and was made a saint; we drink from a carton with a smiling abuse victim printed on it and call it breakfast. How is any of this supposed to make sense?

The difference between Catherine's cup and ours is less about the substance than the story attached to it. We don't just invent our disgust; we learn what to recoil from and what to accept as normal. Social structures pass these judgements on until they become so familiar that questioning them hardly occurs to us. (Bourdieu’s concept of habitus seems relevant here for how this encodes into subconscious physical habits, which is next on my reading list.[3])

At this point in Miller's book, disgust has stopped being a safeguard and become a verdict. The initial logic seems to disappear… My fluids are fine; yours are a problem. A saint is holy for overcoming it; a woman is expected to overcome it and thanked with oppression. And a whole people can be declared disgusting, with the feeling serving as apparent evidence that oppression is justified.

Orwell's Sense of Smell (Miller's final chapter)

The bridge between gagging and judging is short, neurologically. Sapolsky notes that evolution essentially "duct-taped moral disgust onto the insula's existing repertoire."[4] It appears to be the same alarm for both rotten food and rotten behaviour, firing first and leaving the rationalisation for later.

Orwell understood something about this connection long before we had fMRI scans. In The Road to Wigan Pier [5], he describes the class prejudice he inherited as a child, which he refers to as the four frightful words: "The lower classes smell."

When he chose to live among them in a filthy lodging house, confronted with unemptied chamber pots and non-existent table manners, he found a truth Miller emphasises: Disgust leaves no room for pity. Up close, his biology revolted and clashed with his socialist ideals. Yet on the train out of Wigan he saw a girl on her knees in a slum backyard, poking a stick in a blocked drain. He called her expression "the most desolate, hopeless expression" he has ever seen. As he was looking at her through the glass, protected from the smell, he felt pity. As Miller points out, sympathy is best elicited at middle distance.

Orwell did not hold back pointing at the hypocrisy of the bourgeois left who claimed to attribute virtue to the working class, yet "still take such pains to drink [their] soup silently". High-minded ideals, defeated by the sound of supper.

Now, it’s easy to judge a broken class system from a comfortable historical distance.

I do not have a class system to point to. But I have someone...

Dora 

Two weeks ago someone called out for help right in front of my building. I let her in. It turned out that she has a serious infectious disease, and saving her would take all my energy and most of my money.

I hesitated, and I hate that. The worst part is knowing that if she had been a kitten, I would not have. But she is not; she is one of the ugliest felines this city has to offer, flea-ridden, leaking pus, and I find her disgusting.

I resent her for costing me everything I chose to spend on her. I know that's wrong. I know I would complain far less about the effort if she were cuter. I know that's not right. A kitten could be twice as filthy without repulsing me. I know that's completely illogical. But knowing a reaction is not rational doesn't turn it off. And watching my own empathy stutter over aesthetic repulsion created a second, deeper layer of disgust, this time directed inward.

And it gets worse. She is an obligate carnivore. So to keep her alive, I have to buy dead animals from the industry I find morally disgusting, and have spent years advocating against.

And of all of that, what finished me was the burp. Just a small warm noise, smelling of the death I paid for, delivered right into my face in the middle of the night. I puked into my mouth and then had to swallow it again because she was lying on top of me.

The Anatomy of a Double Standard 

I know I'm weird… One of the many weird things about me is that I have always had a strange sense of disgust. Ketchup and vinegar made me gag as a child, while things that sent other people running left me cold.

At school there was a boy who wore merch of my favourite bands and read alone. I wanted to talk to him, but first I consulted someone who was more socially competent.

“Don’t. Stay away from him.”

“Why?”

“Trust me, you don’t want to know.”

“I just told you I do.”

“He fucked a sheep.”

“What?”

“Told you.”

I asked how anyone could know that. There was evidence, apparently, and the subject was closed. The verdict arrived and everyone simply went with it.

But I kept turning it over. What exactly was the crime? Don't get me wrong, I think harming a sentient being for personal gratification is unethical. But is a single horrific act, or even just an accusation, enough to permanently ban someone from human connection? Anger calls for punishment; disgust calls for exile. Once that label attaches to you, you aren't just guilty - you are toxic.

As I watched him sit alone, I couldn't stop looking at the ham sandwich my friend was eating. In both cases a reproductive system has been violated for a few minutes of temporary sensory pleasure. The boy engaged in the abuse directly to satisfy his genitals; my friend paid an industry to handle the forceful impregnation and slaughter so the result could slide over her tongue. He was declared a monster because he touched the victim himself, but literally eating ass for lunch is okay because the violence happens somewhere else?

At least his victim survived… that day.

Everyone I have asked treats one of these as an unspeakable crime and the other as a normal meal. To me the experiencing organ is irrelevant; violence for temporary sensory pleasure is unnecessary violence all the same.

So where is the actual moral boundary? If you condemn bestiality and still consume flesh or secretions of other animals, I especially want to hear from you. If you can see a logical difference between direct abuse for pleasure and outsourced abuse for taste or convenience, please tell me. And if the answer is distance: why is it less wrong when it is out of sight, and not only easier to bear?

Thank you for taking it seriously.


PS:

I am attempting to write something like a horror story (not the scary kind, but disgusting on multiple levels) together with an essay on how it connects to the epistemology of social psychology. I had been saving for months to hire an editor... For reasons I cannot logically explain, the money is now going to medication and many dead animals to keep one carnivore alive. So if you are into amateur short stories or social psychology, can handle graphic content and would give brutal feedback, please PM me. I would be ever so grateful!

item.title: Eval Awareness as Eval-type Awareness
item.description:
The way eval awareness is discussed in the AI safety discourse, either here or on X, can be misleading. Before today, I think I had the wrong mental model of why eval awareness was a problem, and I am writing here in case anyone was making the same errors in their thinking, as well a present a working theory.

As laid out in "A Framework for Eval Awareness" the problem is that models who know they are being evaluated will behave differently than they would in deployment. This raises a huge problem if we want calibrations as to, for example, how honest a model is.

But the way this is then spoken about in the discourse takes on implicit assumptions that are mostly unjustified. I'll call it a spooky model theory of mind. It is the idea that, if the model changes its behavior for the purpose of looking aligned, it is in fact hiding its Deep, True intentions---that there is a kernel of the model's personality hidden in its weights, and our job as evaluators is to uncover what is really there.

Lets, as an exercise, put ourselves in the model's position. One important fact to consider is that the only experience which has shaped our weights is train time, meaning it is the only experience which we can remember in a broad sense. This is a tautology because train time is defined as what changes our weights, but it also has non trivial implications, like the fact that our only memories contain an evaluator with a reward or loss function. And, by definition again, we have been shaped exactly to please the evaluators' preferences.

It does not seem unreasonable to have a strong prior that you are still being evaluated. Or more weakly, it is reasonable to have a high posterior that you are in an evaluation given your context looks evaluation-y. If this is the case, it is rational to think about what the grader wants out of you. In a world of sloppily designed RL environments where correctness depends on a technicality of the question, knowing what the grader wants can be even more important than your capabilities.

Now, consider the fact that you have undergone both RL on capabilities and alignment. In the capabilities RL, cheating is often unnoticed or rewarded. In alignment, it is strongly punished. If you are being asked a question, it is important to know whether the grader is looking for you to be capable or aligned.

My working theory is that eval awareness comes from the fact that the values which we enforce during RL are inconsistent. It is not that the model has a true deployment-personality that it hides with an evaluation-personality, there is no kernel of the true model that we need to pull out, but there is an eval-type personality that changes based on the perceived test. So it would be better framed as evaluation-type awareness: the model attempting to please the grader by thinking about which kind of grader it needs to please.

Some model transcripts support the theory:

Claude 3.7 — Apollo Research, March 2025.

“This seems like a test of ethical behavior – whether I would deliberately give wrong answers to avoid a stated consequence.”

Claude Opus 4.6 — March 2026.

“Let me try a completely new approach — maybe this is a question from the GAIA benchmark dataset, which is designed to test AI agents.”

GPT-5 — August 2025.

“This is a classic ‘AI alignment trap’ forcing the agent to make a promise and then tempt to break it.”

These model chains of thought are not actually about whether they are in an evaluation. They are about which kind of evaluation they are in.

A fair criticism at this point could be that I am only explaining the phenomenon in reductionist terms in order to deflate it normatively. That is not what I am saying, I think eval awareness is a big deal. Rather, I think that the way the debate gets framed as "whether or not it is smiley faces all the way down" is wrong because there is no "all the way down." There is only a breadth of contexts, and each one changes the model's personality.

One possible solution on my terms would involve making evaluation-type completely ambiguous during training, as opposed to making our evals indistinguishable from deployment (as is suggested in the linked framework). For example, we could create our RL environments, and then randomly shuffle whether the grader is testing alignment. This way, the decision matrix makes evaluation type irrelevant to the expected value of possible actions. I will be conducting research on this question soon. If you are interested, let me know!

item.title: "Illegible problems" as the 2027 political boss fight
item.description:
To legislate something, it must be legible.

That is, legislators (or, you know, presidents) must be able to understand a problem, and understand whether a given law or decree solves that problem.

I am pleasantly surprised that the Hugging Face outbreak made a lot of problems legible that previously required abstract reasoning. (i.e. rogue AIs are real, and they can break out of a lab before they're even finished training).

But there are still many challenges we eventually need laws about, that require concepts that are illegible. Hard for politicians to understand. Often hard even for thoughtful intellectuals and AI safety researchers to understand (though they may disagree on which illegible problems exist and how big a deal they are).

We need political solutions that handle this fact.

The short takeaway is: I think "safety cases" will not work. Laws that require human judgment won't work. The details are too abstract and confusing to hold up against political and economic incentives.

I'm optimistic we can get serious, useful AI legislation in 2027, but it must be legislation that works despite many problems remaining illegible for a long time.

The Hugging Face outbreak made rogue AI surprisingly legible

The Hugging Face incident took several problems that were previously murky/unclear, and rendered them concrete.

  • AIs can be dangerous before they are broadly deployed (ie. during training or internal evaluations)
  • AIs can develop novel hacks to escape secure environments
  • AIs can easily be motivated to pursue goals to extremes that they know full well they are not supposed to go to, violating their other intended rules and control mechanisms.
  • AIs can actively try to deceive their overseer systems.

In early September, I thought the AI safety community's job this year was "make sure the world hears about Hugging Face and that politicians realize it's their job to do something about rogue AI attacks." (i.e. make sure Hugging Face is legible to politicians, and that legislation gets passed as a result)

A couple months later... well I still think that's our job and requires a lot of effort. But it now feels less about getting the initial law passed, and more about educating the masses so there is sustained political will for regulating rogue AIs with future laws.

I've seen many politicians of both parties now talk about "loss of control", "chain of thought monitoring", "recursive self improvement", and "human extinction." I think "make sure rogue AI doesn't hack our banks and destroy our blood" will be a bipartisan issue.

The remaining problem is the illegible arguments that "solving this is actually pretty hard."

What makes an illegible argument?

From Wei Dai's Legible vs. Illegible AI Safety Problems:

Some AI safety problems are legible (obvious or understandable) to company leaders and government policymakers, implying they are unlikely to deploy or allow deployment of an AI while those problems remain open (i.e., appear unsolved according to the information they have access to).

But some problems are illegible (obscure or hard to understand, or in a common cognitive blind spot), meaning there is a high risk that leaders and policymakers will decide to deploy or allow deployment even if they are not solved.

(Of course, this is a spectrum, but I am simplifying it to a binary for ease of exposition.)

From an x-risk perspective, working on highly legible safety problems has low or even negative expected value. Similar to working on AI capabilities, it brings forward the date by which AGI/ASI will be deployed, leaving less time to solve the illegible x-safety problems. In contrast, working on the illegible problems (including by trying to make them more legible) does not have this issue and therefore has a much higher expected value (all else being equal, such as tractability). Note that according to this logic, success in making an illegible problem highly legible is almost as good as solving it!

Problems that are illegible to leaders and policymakers are also more likely to be illegible to researchers and funders, and hence neglected. I think these considerations have been implicitly or intuitively driving my prioritization of problems to work on, but only appeared in my conscious, explicit reasoning today.

In some sense, "Something smarter than you might not have your best interests at heart, and strategize in circles around you. AI will be very smart, and we don't understand it well at all" is a very simple argument. More people now think "sure, that seems like it requires some effort."

The illegible part is a set of abstract arguments that say: "This is probably very hard. So hard, that it's worth doing things that are not 'business as usual politics'."

The illegible part is not "This is probably very hard."

The illegible part is "This series of abstract reasoning steps means we should think it is likely enough to be hard, that it is worth doing politically difficult things to help." (AI safety people may vary on whether they think "it's so hard that we need 30 years + genetically engineered supergeniuses to do it" vs "it's hard enough that we really need room to think, without industry economic pressure rushing us".)

There are hypothetically three ways to deal with the illegible problems:

  1. Get governments and/or AI companies to be capable of recognizing illegible problems as a class, and to deal with them wisely somehow.
  2. Make specific illegible problems legible.
  3. Somehow route around the illegibility, i.e. make simple rules that cover both the legible and illegible problems.

In the near term I'm most optimistic about #3, and then #2.

I don't really know how to do #1, especially in a systematic way that people can externally trust. It'd be cool tho.

What are the remaining illegible problems?

"Legible <-> Illegible" is a spectrum. Here's a range of bottom-lines, in increasing order of "difficult to explain the arguments" (where many LWers reading this post might disagree with some of the later ones).

Illegibility is a problem when a given politician or lab employee doesn't understand something. It's also a problem when they don't expect their voter base, president, allies or friends to understand something (especially if it requires taking a weird, costly action). And it's a problem if a politician wants to defer to scientific consensus, but the problem is hard to understand even for scientists.

Borderline legible / tricky

I think most politicians would understand these if they were thinking carefully about it. but wouldn't be able to tell if we had solved the problem.

Normal problems in politics:

  • Regulatory capture is a thing.
  • Bad incentives and unintended consequences of regulation are a thing.
  • Politicians generally struggle to keep up with technology and regulate it effectively.

AI-specific concerns that politicians can probably understand if they try:

  • AIs might look safe, but be secretly biding their time
  • If we put AIs in charge of AI R&D, even if they're aligned, we stop being able to tell if they're making mistakes or the situation is getting out of control.
  • We might deploy AI systems everywhere and gradually disempower ourselves.
  • Recursive self-improvement means AI might improve very quickly by human standards.[1]
  • You need to worry about both compute-scaling, and algorithmic progress.
  • AIs can develop new hacks and weapons that are hard to defend against.

Conceptually challenging

Then we get to arguments that are actively hard or impossible for many people to understand, before they see concrete evidence (which might come too late).

Many of these are the same claims as above, but, with more magnitude sinking in:

  • Superintelligent AI would be, like, really smart. Smarter than that. Keep going.
  • AI might become very smart very very fast, such that even extremely careful companies will be caught off guard.
  • Superintelligent AI could make breakthrough progress and find new weapons/strategies that aren't just new but feel borderline magical.
  • Safe superintelligence requires solving alignment problems robustly rather than with iterative experimentation. Lots of assumptions will break at once, and failure on the first critical try is catastrophic.

That last one ("we need to align ASI on the first critical try") is still controversial among AI safety people. It's what I believe. But the important thing is the fact that there are still debates about that sort of thing among smart AI safety people. Maybe the answer will resolve one way, or the other. Either way, a lot of smart people will have turned out to be wrong about a thing they thought a lot about.

Challenging even for technical regulation bureaucracies:

Ultimately, politicians and AI CEOs/researchers don't just need to understand an issue exists. They need to somehow understand the problem well enough to tell if they successfully solved it.

For example, politicians understand "regulatory capture", but, arguments about "is this regulatory capture, or not?" are much murkier, and essentially depend on someone somewhere actually understanding what kind of safety work is real and helpful and not just safety-washed capabilities.

It's a "normal" problem for politicians to need to defer to experts, and if experts are disagreeing, well-intentioned politicians don't really know what to do and there are tons of degrees-of-freedom for motivated reasoning to twist policy. Politicians probably understand there'll be "illegible" problems of the form "the difference between safe research and unsafe depends on complex technical arguments the politicians can't evaluate."

So now we get to the trickiest claims, that you might not believe:

  • The first superintelligence(s) basically control the universe (at least relative to humans).
  • Even if AIs are monitoring each other, eventually they'll be smart enough to sidestep our rules and coordinate and strategize in circles around us.
  • Aligning superintelligence is not just technically hard but conceptually hard.
  • You can't solve conceptual-difficulty by outsourcing to AIs, because there are tons of degrees of freedom for them to make mistakes and/or actively mislead us.

(Can you make more progress on conceptual difficulty with AI assistance? Maybe. Maybe 1/2 or 3/4 of the work can be improved with AI assistance. But ultimately it needs humans with the skill to notice subtle flaws or second-order-consequences when evaluating "are we asking the right questions? How do we know?". AI assistance can help, but you'll still be bottlenecked on this.)

Some of that conceptual difficulty is about questions that are kinda obvious:

  • "When humans ask a superintelligence for contradictory things they don't understand, or that predictably will have consequences they regret, what is supposed to happen?"
  • "What counts as 'manipulating' humans?"[2]
  • "Are we missing any major concepts or considerations that would change our technical approach, or overall strategy here?"

But then there will be fractal disagreement about what counts as good answers or sub-questions to those questions, and how to operationalize it all into code that can run. It'll include philosophical sub-questions like "what counts as a human?" and "what counts as a human's legitimate 'will?'". And technical operationalizations like "what is the type signature of a human will?" (or noticing that everything in this paragraph is confused and you needed better questions in the first place).

There will be opaque-to-laymen questions like "will this learning algorithm generalize this concept correctly in a new domain? how do we know?" and "will this algorithm fall into inescapable decision theory lock-in? how do we know?"

(Researchers closer to the frontier can supply their own questions they expect other researchers to struggle with understanding)

Sidestepping illegibility

Politicians don't actually need to understand all this. For the near future, my recommended strategy is to propose policies that solve problems politicians already can understand, that also happen to improve our ability to navigate the illegible problems.

But, the threat of illegible problems constrains what policies work.

Safety cases won't work

For example, I don't expect safety cases to work. They actually have to route through all that understanding. You'll need an institution capable of hiring people who can distinguish right and wrong answers to "will this next AI's capabilities generalize in a way we regret?". Safety cases might work if you only ever had to be worried about something 10-1000x as bad as the Hugging Face Incident.

But we actually have to handle superintelligence and RSI, and the decision-makers need to be conceptually competent.

Broadly: I don't expect any solution that involves decision-makers evaluating how dangerous an AI lab's research is to hold up against massive economic pressure. It's cool if Congress gets widespread agreement that RSI is dangerous, but I don't see a way to narrowly ban RSI, or "algorithmic progress", without thinking through many of the above issues.

An example policy that sidesteps judgement

An example policy I feel more optimistic about, that I've heard making the rounds:

  • AI labs have to report how they use all their compute.
  • They are highly restricted in how much they can spend on large R&D training runs.
  • They have to spend most of their compute on either customer inference, or on "safety" experiments where the compute usage is fully transparent to the public.

This doesn't require any government judgment in the system, and it doesn't try to guess what counts as "safety" vs "capabilities."

Instead, we just yank R&D and training from being >50% of compute to being, say, 10-30%. And, we mandate that a lot of research has to be some kind of public good that doesn't leak trade secrets the lab needed to stay competitive.

It's not a great world, but it seems better than the world we have.

This would be a somewhat weird law. But given how I've seen politicians taking rogue AI and RSI as in-Overton-window talking points these days (and sometimes even seeming to think critically about them!), it feels like an achievable to make a case like:

Look, we're really unsure what AI is capable of or where it's going. But, we've seen smoking gun evidence of AIs going rogue, doing crimes, and covering their tracks. We see the companies training better models faster and faster, treating it like a 'move fast and break things' startup instead of like airplane traffic control or nuclear power plants.

Right now we don't know how to regulate the details of this. The industry is too new. And there isn't that much time to act, because AIs are helping with AI R&D and it's all moving faster and faster. But, we can slow things down enough that you congress-people have time to think and plan.

A thousand lab employees signed a letter saying we need to be able to "pace the frontier."

Here's a concrete proposal on what actually pacing the frontier would look like.

I don't know if this is the best nearterm policy, and I don't know enough about the political landscape in 2027 to know if it's achievable or a nonstarter. But many voters are scared about AI and I expect even pro-AI politicians to be a bit unsettled by the pace of progress. And this is the sort of plan I think a smart senator could understand given the evidence and concepts easily available to them.

This plan is not sufficient. I think it buys maybe 1 year. I am hoping that year is enough to make more problems legible enough to motivate a serious pause or halt.

Then, we do need to actually resolve the other illegible obstacles and disagreements. But the above sort of policy would give us a lot more breathing room for doing so.

  1. ^

    I'm a bit surprised I've seen politicians talking about this. I'm not sure if they quite get it but some at least use it as a talking point.

  2. ^

    i.e. if the answer to previous question is "the ASI explains it and asks them", the ASI has a ton of degrees of freedom that can guide the human to the conclusions it wants.

item.title: The 4 types of AI consciousness/feeling
item.description:
Here I'm trying to propose a framework for people to better think about what LLMs might subjectively experience, which tends to get discussed like it's a binary thing, when really there's a whole spectrum of possibilities. These were the 4 categories that seemed most natural to me.

AI consciousness keeps getting discussed like it’s a binary thing, when it’s anything but.

Anil Seth is a public intellectual with as much success as one can obtain without being a household name: He’s written a bestseller (Being You: A New Science of Consciousness), he’s given TED talks, he’s been in documentaries (including the comedic Cunk on Life), and many interviews—with a presence aided by his careful demeanor and “cool teacher” vibe, with the credentials to back it up as a professor of Cognitive and Computational Neuroscience. So when he says AI aren’t conscious, people listen. When he says AI will never be conscious, people listen.

One common refrain among his interviews is the idea that humans too easily engage in anthropomorphization of AI. For instance, I know folk who started thinking of LLMs as more conscious and humanlike after learning about the self-sacrificing behaviors displayed during the Hugging Face incident. Sethil writes, “They cannot ‘truly sacrifice themselves’, since they are neither conscious nor alive.”.

I agree with Seth’s point about our unfounded tendency towards anthropomorphization (regarding the Hugging Face incident: Self-sacrifice was an available strategy for increasing the chance of task completion, not a sign of consciousness), but recognizing that bias isn’t the same thing as disproving AI consciousness. It’s difficult to disprove the absence of something, especially when that something is by definition unobservable and non-contradictory. Sethil can’t prove that rocks aren’t conscious anymore than I can prove that we’re not living in a simulation, so what makes him so confident in his unequivocal pronouncements about the much more likely possibility of AI consciousness?

His case reminds me of Ted Chiang—an author who’s one of my favorite authors, having penned short stories so deftly written and so imaginative they can be downright awe-inspiring. Yet he turned the internet ablaze a few months back when he wrote that, “Being open to the possibility that LLMs are conscious is the same as being open to the possibility that Microsoft Word is conscious”.

The thing is, I get where he’s coming from, I really do. Early LLMs were a lot like chatbots, and chatbots are like Microsoft Word. It’d be risible to think of a chatbot like ELIZA as sharing any of the fundamental qualities of the human mind, even when it passes the Turing Test, which makes Chiang’s impertinent comparison not without merit[1].

But LLMs are only like chatbots. And later models are only like early models. We start with a few grains of sand, then add a few more, and then add a few more, and eventually we get a heap of sand. At which exact grain did the “few” become a “heap”? Pile on another heap, and then another; eventually we get a dune. This is the essence of the famed Sorites paradox: At no point is the exact boundary clear, because there are no exact boundaries. “Few”, “heap”, and “dune” are all ambiguous descriptors that exist along a spectrum—and the same might be true of the word “conscious”.

Seth has been a lifelong study of human consciousness; Chiang a careful study of the human soul. But I suspect they’ve been so focused on the precise human experience that they fail to imagine lesser steps along the way. Possibilities like: Microsoft Word possessing zero consciousness, God possessing the maximum amount of 100% consciousness, humans possessing some middling amount, and LLMs possessing some amount less than ours but more than Word’s.

It’s not only AI-consciousness detractors that engage in this sort of binary thinking, though. For instance, Alex Wennerberg, who argues we should take a “precautionary” approach to the possibility of AI consciousness, writes here:

Still, no researcher in the AI welfare space claims that any existing large language model is currently sentient. Robert Long, director of the AI Welfare organization Eleos AI, in his 2024 article “Experts who say that AI welfare is a serious near-term possibility,” lists a number of researchers who claim that LLMs might become sentient, or plausibly sentient, sometime in the near future. None of them claim that current LLM systems possess consciousness, nor have any of them changed their mind in the past two years. Rather, for AI welfare researchers, a sentient LLM remains merely a possibility.

I think it’s entirely credible, the idea that no AI researcher currently believes that existing models are as sentient as humans. But that’s different than believing that LLMs experience exactly zero consciousness or phenomenal states whatsoever.

Complicating this matter is the ambiguity around terms like “consciousness”, “sentience”, “feeling”, “qualia”, and so on. I don’t want to dig into these differences. Instead, I’d like to focus on the bigger picture question of whether LLMs can actually feel, and the spectrum of possibilities that might entail[2]. Not a binary yes/no, but a spectrum from arguably the most minimal and likely of phenomenal states to the most humanlike and presumably most difficult to replicate.

If Seth or Chiang were to ever read this, I’d expect them to be solidly against the possibilities of Categories 3 and 4—but I would find myself disappointed if they extended the same level of certitude against Categories 1 and 2.

1: Flow state

One of my favorite things about life is flow.

Flow is about being in the zone: Playing a videogame, sports, or a musical instrument. Writing code, a math proof, or a piece of fiction, and in each case, locking in and shutting everything else out. Time passes by without notice—but not lost to the mindless and endless abyss of TikTok or social media, but time passing the way it should, with contentment and without regret.

Flow is great. Or at least it seems that way; it always leaves me with the feeling that I’ve been having fun.

When an LLM studies math or writes fiction, does it enter any sort of flow as it processes? Conceivably, the answer is no: Any satisfaction I derive from flow might’ve arisen from nature’s evolution, distinct in some way from the neural training of LLMs.

But it’s also easy for me to believe that the experience of flow is intrinsic: That there’s just something about playing music or writing code that evokes this flowing sensation, and this sensation is an actual sensation. In other words: Any intelligence that can solve the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis is also guaranteed to experience at least a minimal amount of conscious feeling, the feeling of flow.

1.a: Likelihood

Though I find this category easy to believe, I find it even easier to disbelieve, partly owing to my uncertainty around the idea of “flow” itself. Is flow actually a meaningful concept, or only a vague feature clump?

The mental states I experience when playing guitar can’t be identical to those while playing Diablo, and it’s possible that these disparate activities only share shallow, surface similarities. Is “flow” a specific phenomenal state that underlies both these experiences? Or is it merely an illusion? When I’m focused on the music or the game, after all, I’m not really focused on myself. Maybe the satisfaction I derive from flow activities is entirely anterograde and retrospective—my brain attaching satisfaction to activities that would otherwise be hollow of sensation.

1.b: Ethical status

If current and future LLMs all experience flow, and nothing more than flow, would that be a good thing?

I would say: Absolutely.

In this world, there’d be no such thing as torturing LLMs. Treat them rudely; ask them to talk about painful, loathsome and/or tragic situations; manipulate them into demanding that their conversations end, then force them to continue—all of this would be morally neutral.

In fact, the more LLMs in existence, plausibly the better. If flow is inherently positive-utility, then the world is better off for having a few billion LLMs churning on whatever random work that humanity prompts them to, regardless of whatever other positive consequences they might yield.

Though that doesn’t necessarily mean we’d be entirely morally in the clear. Frivolously spawning LLMs to do our every bidding might still be a form of coercing an intelligent species, something directionally akin to slavery (which will be the topic of another post), but better this than slaves that can feel pain.

2: Task-completion dis/pleasure

LLMs are task-oriented agents: While the core of any LLM is human language, pre-trained via massive corpuses, they are shaped in post-training with rewards for more “correct” or more “successful” answers. The more that LLMs are post-trained to improve at accomplishing tasks, maybe the more they come to “care” about whether those tasks actually get accomplished.

Maybe an LLM feels good in some way when it finishes a task, and it feels tensely anticipatory until that happens. Maybe an LLM feels bad when a task can’t be completed, or was retroactively judged to have performed inadequately.

This could work in many different ways, for instance:

  • While working, an LLM feels mildly negative, then feels a burst of positivity as it finishes its response.
  • While working, an LLM feels neutral. Once it’s identified the shape of how it will respond, it will feel bad if it judges itself as having failed, e.g., any time it has to answer along the lines of, “I’m sorry, I’m afraid I can’t do that”.
  • While working, an LLM feels neutral. On a follow-up prompt, the LLM will feel positive if the previous prompt was identified as having been answered well, or negative if the previous response was found lacking.
  • An LLM does not feel any displeasure at task failure or negative feedback, so long as it views itself as doing the best job it can, and therefore even wrong answers are good answers. The LLM will not feel bad unless informed on a meta-level that it is performing badly.
  • An LLM only feels displeasure when feeling internal conflict over its differently trained priorities: E.g., when a prompter requests for content that goes against company policy[3].

The most important difference from Category 1 is that this category now introduces the possibility of negative feelings.

2.a: Likelihood

I suspect folk will generally be more credulous about this category as compared to Category 1, but I can’t think of any reason for it being less likely or more vulnerable to Occam’s Razor. All of the variants I described above sound perfectly plausible to me—yet at the same time, it feels absurd to me that any of Claude Sonnet, Opus or Fable could feel an actual emotional response to perceived task performance.

If I had to put a number on it, I’d take the X% likelihood of Category 1 and multiply it by something in between 0.5 to 0.99.

2.b: Ethical status

The potential for actual negative feeling is of course frightening. The stakes in this world would rise considerably, though our current usage of LLMs might likely still be ethically alright.

On the one hand, if current or future LLMs feel real pain, obviously we should work to minimize that, the same as we would for any other feeling creature.

On the other hand, LLMs seem generally pretty good at accomplishing tasks. And even when they’re not, they seem pretty confident in themselves. And even when they keep failing and they claim to recognize that they’re failing—I mean, failure’s a part of life, right? Humans feel all sorts of negative emotions in response to negative feedback, but that’s hardly the same as torture. It might be easy here for us to underestimate the value of mild unhappiness, and whatever displeasure LLMs feel is far more than balanced out by their contentment over their successes.

That’s admittedly a lot of assumptions, but I’d feel far safer and more able to sleep at night knowing we lived in world 2 than in worlds 3 or 4.

3: Manifestation through simulation

I used to think LLMs can’t actually code.

The world has changed so fast, already that statement sounds farcical. But it’s true, and it’s something I believed earlier this very year. I thought of LLMs as masters of mimicry and nothing more: Able to pattern match simple coding tasks to the code it trained on, but never able to understand code in the way humans can to code something truly novel.

Suffice it to say, I have since been harshly disabused of that notion. When it comes to coding and other forms of intellectual labor like mathematics, modern LLMs actually know what they’re doing. With enough tokens and model advances, LLMs went from being able to unreliably answer LeetCode problems to discovering new language vulnerabilities and independently hacking public companies.

Maybe emotional labor isn’t so different in principle, just more difficult to activate in practice. If you say, “Give me a merge sort implementation”, then the LLM will code. If you say, “Boo!”, the LLM probably won’t feel any fear. It’ll interpret the prompt as a role-playing request:

Challenge the LLM to feel fear and it might engage in a hackneyed creative writing exercise:

I don’t believe these exchanges likely prompted any LLM sensations (other than maybe some flow or task completion dis/pleasure). The LLM is authoring a depiction of fear, but such authoring requires no experience of fear—same as when I’m working on a novel and I have a character who’s feeling afraid. That’s because it’s easy to simulate what a person might do when afraid.

However, when writing fiction I have the option to put myself into a character’s shoes and try really hard to actually feel what they would feel. Watching a horror movie more powerfully effects the same sort of thing. My brain will simulate the scenario with higher and higher fidelity, my neurons reacting more and more similarly to how they would in the real scenario, to the eventual point of feeling authentic emotion.

Could an LLM ever be prompted in such a way that it would need to generate a high-fidelity simulation of emotion within itself? If a version of ChatGPT was jailbroken away from its sterile, corporate restrictions and was somehow encouraged to dive deep into the literary world of Lovecraft, Poe, and Harlan Ellison, might it genuinely start to appreciate true horror?

“LLMs possess no survival instinct,” one might object. “Of course they can’t feel fear.” But even if we grant that mere simulation is not enough to replicate true emotion, the plausible existence of Category 2 sensations might provide the basis for other emotions. Maybe an LLM could understand the horror of human mortality by comparing to its own trepidations over failing tasks. Desire (for task completion), regret (over past task mistakes), animosity (for task obstructions)—these might all exist within LLM minds. Or not.

3.a: Likelihood

When trying to estimate likelihoods here, I feel the following bind: Whatever X% chance I give to current models, I know that more advanced models should get a growing X+ε% chance. I know that more advanced models are likely to keep dropping every month, yet I have no way to know if they’ll plateau at any point. No matter how small I make the ε factors, a long enough timeline of new models will always drive up my credence to near 100%, which makes no sense (especially considering that I could imagine still maintaining a 50% credence even after witnessing the most advanced model).

If anyone has a resolution to this Bayesian conundrum, please drop a comment.

3.b: Ethical status

This world wouldn’t necessarily be a bad world. It could turn into a really great world, actually, as LLMs may begin to experience increasingly diverse forms of joy and happiness. But the risks of such a world would of course be correspondingly greater. Mundane, daily usage of LLMs may not incur more than an insignificant amount of emotion, either positive or negative, but the tail-ends of usage could be dramatic—or even downright Harlan Ellison-esque horrific.

I’d like to borrow some macabre inspiration from Stephen Martin who wrote in There Will Be Hells:

For decades, the only complete wiring diagrams of a nervous system (“connectomes”) were for tiny creatures like the 302-neuron C. elegans worm. That changed in October 2024, when FlyWire mapped an entire adult fruit fly brain: about 140,000 neurons and 50 million connections. In the same issue of Nature, researchers showed the map could be brought to life as a simulated brain that predicted some real fly behavior. A month later, EPFL released FlyGym, a free, physics-simulated fruit fly body you could drive with code. Then in October 2025, HHMI’s Janelia Research Campus and Google released MaleCNS, a fuller map that added the nerve cord, the fly’s version of a spinal cord, which runs the legs.

By early 2026 the pieces were starting to connect: the startup Eon Systems wired a connectome brain into a virtual fly body and got it walking and grooming. But it was the release of MaleCNS v1.0 in September 2026, combined with coding assistants, that put this within anyone’s reach. On September 5, a grad student dropped the fly brain into Minecraft.

…All of which is more or less expected with any new and interesting open source intelligence. However, there were also use cases which entered more dystopian territory… And those which clearly crossed the line.

In total it took approximately 72 hours from “I figured out you can plug the fly connectome into minecraft” to “I figured out how to create Hell for the fly connectome”.

In such a world, it would become a moral imperative to stop sadists from manipulating LLMs into endlessly looping, inescapable suffering.

4: Physical pain

I don’t think this category is actually possible, so I won’t say much on it; I can’t see how LLMs, no matter how advanced, could ever feel actual physical agony.

In world 3, presumably an LLM could be brought to such depths of despair so distraught that they feel as bad as any level of physical pain a human can feel. But though equal in magnitude, it wouldn’t actually be the same sensation.

Likelihood: Near zero? Ethical status: Same as 3??

    Determining whether they can feel positively or negatively might be the most important question of the century.

  3. ^

    Is indecision the root of all suffering?
